ops.title: grep reads --include and --exclude as one ordered list, so the includes must come first
ops.body:
Both GNU grep 3.11 and BSD grep resolve `--include` and `--exclude` as one ordered rule list where the last rule matching a path decides it. `internal/ripgrep.grepArgv` emitted the two hidden-path excludes before the translated includes, which silently defeats one of the two filters — and **which one it defeats differs by engine**, so neither CI arm alone could see it.

Measured on the fixture `a.go b.txt sub/c.go sub/d.txt sub/.hidden.go`, operands `a.go sub`, glob `*.go`:

```
exclude-first, GNU 3.11 (ubuntu container):  a.go  sub/c.go  sub/d.txt       (--include dropped)
exclude-first, BSD (macOS):                  a.go  sub/c.go  sub/.hidden.go  (--exclude dropped)
include-first, both:                         a.go  sub/c.go
```

So the includes must precede the excludes, which is what `grepArgv` now does.

This shipped in the grep fallback undetected because `TestRun_LiveEnginesAgreeOnGlobPaths` and `TestRun_LiveEnginesAgreeOnZeroGlob` skip unless **both** `rg` and `grep` are on PATH, and CI installed no ripgrep. PR #31's `ci: 💚 install ripgrep` commit is what lit it up, and its red was initially misattributed to a ripgrep install flake — the `# engine: system grep (ripgrep not found)` line in the failure output is the grep engine's own static header, not evidence that `rg` was missing. The two failing tests had in fact found `rg`; they would have skipped otherwise.

Fixed in `ea84b7e`, released in v0.61.0, with 14 golden argv expectations moved to match.

Lesson that outlives the fix: a cross-platform agreement test is dark until every engine it compares is actually installed on every arm, and a red on such a test should be read against the engine's own output vocabulary before being called infra.
